articles.title: Telehealth-related education and training: a systematic review of recent developments since the COVID-19 pandemic.
articles.dek: A systematic review identified 51 telehealth education programs developed since 2020, mostly in US universities and targeting undergraduates, but found most curricula lack comprehensive coverage of ethical, legal, and clinical competencies.
summary: This systematic review examined telehealth-related education and training programs implemented between 2020 and 2024. The authors searched available literature and included 51 articles from 7,547 identified records that described specific program content or learning objectives for any educational level or health professional type. Quality assessment used SQUIRE 2.0 guidelines, and learning objectives were mapped to six Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC) telehealth competency domains.

Most programs (82%) were implemented in the USA, developed by universities (53%), and targeted undergraduate students (51%), with increasing publication frequency over the review period. Participants evaluated courses in 90% of programs. Course content typically included basic telehealth knowledge and skills, patient safety, and ethics, with particular emphasis on technology and communication competencies. Only four of 51 programs included all six AAMC telehealth competencies.

The authors concluded that while telehealth education has expanded since the COVID-19 pandemic onset, current curricula are limited by lack of experiential learning and insufficient coverage of ethical and legal requirements, billing, physical examination techniques, patient education, and telehealth eligibility criteria. The review suggests standardized training applicable across disciplines with specialty-specific modules could improve resource efficiency.
articles.why: These findings are relevant to medical educators and healthcare system leaders designing workforce development in telehealth delivery. The gap between existing training programs and comprehensive competency frameworks may inform curriculum development discussions, particularly regarding clinical skills assessment and regulatory compliance in remote care. However, this review describes current educational offerings without determining optimal training approaches or patient outcomes associated with different curricula.

evidence.design: Systematic literature review with independent dual data extraction and quality assessment against SQUIRE 2.0 guidelines
evidence.sample: 51 articles included from 7,547 initial records identified; specific numbers of students, trainees, or programs not reported
evidence.limitations: Abstract does not specify literature databases searched, date ranges for inclusion, publication status restrictions, or inter-rater reliability measures. No information provided on whether included studies reported validated competency assessment outcomes. Geographic bias toward USA programs noted. Full paper assessment necessary to evaluate methodological quality and generalizability of findings.
evidence.uncertainty: Reasons for exclusion of 7,496 articles not detailed. Whether identified gaps reflect educational priorities versus resource constraints unknown. No information on follow-up assessment of trainee competency or healthcare delivery outcomes post-training.

articles.title: Child Maltreatment During COVID-19: Triangulating Data Across Reporting Sources.
articles.dek: A systematic review of 73 studies found discordant trends in child maltreatment reporting during COVID-19, with child welfare data suggesting declines but self-report studies documenting increases.
summary: This systematic review used PRISMA criteria to examine changes in child maltreatment rates during the COVID-19 pandemic. Researchers identified 4,193 unique studies and selected 73 that met eligibility criteria. The review triangulated data across three independent surveillance sources: child welfare administrative records, hospital reports, and self-report studies.

Results showed divergent patterns by data source. Child welfare sources reported declining maltreatment rates immediately following COVID-19 onset. In contrast, self-report studies documented increasing trends. Hospital data were largely mixed, with more studies reporting decreased rather than increased child maltreatment during this period.

The authors emphasize that interpretation of child maltreatment surveillance data during COVID-19 must account for evidence from multiple data sources, as different reporting mechanisms can yield substantially different conclusions about population-level trends. The discordance across data sources suggests complex relationships between pandemic stressors and actual versus reported maltreatment.
articles.why: This review is relevant for understanding surveillance challenges in child protection and public health monitoring during crises. The finding that different data sources yield opposite conclusions highlights the importance of multi-method approaches when assessing harm to vulnerable populations. It informs discussion about underreporting in official systems, potential changes in help-seeking behavior, and how policy decisions during emergencies should not rely on a single surveillance stream.

evidence.design: Systematic review using PRISMA methodology; observational, not randomized
evidence.sample_size: 4,193 studies screened; 73 studies meeting eligibility criteria included in analysis
evidence.major_limitations: Abstract does not specify inclusion criteria details, quality assessment methodology, geographic scope, study designs included, or effect sizes for individual findings. Reasons for the discordance between data sources are not explained in the abstract. Full-text assessment of methodological rigor, heterogeneity across studies, and meta-analysis presence or absence cannot be determined from this abstract.

articles.title: Effectiveness of physical, psychological, and alternative interventions for post-COVID-19 condition: a systematic review.
articles.dek: A systematic review of 27 randomized trials found that supervised physical rehabilitation and cognitive-behavioral therapy show promise for improving function and reducing symptoms in post-COVID-19 condition, though most included trials had methodological limitations.
summary: This systematic review evaluated randomized controlled trials of supervised physical, psychological, and alternative non-pharmacological interventions in adults with post-COVID-19 condition as defined by the World Health Organization. The review searched four databases from January 2020 through January 2026 and included 27 trials enrolling 1,998 participants. Risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane RoB 2 methodology.

Supervised cardiopulmonary rehabilitation and multimodal exercise consistently improved cardiorespiratory fitness and walking capacity. Cognitive-behavioral therapy and lifestyle adjustments significantly reduced fatigue and subjective concentration complaints. By contrast, findings for neuromodulation, complementary therapies, and oxygen therapies were heterogeneous and often showed no advantage over placebo or control conditions.

The authors concluded that supervised physical rehabilitation and CBT demonstrate promising evidence for improving functional capacity and symptoms in post-COVID-19 condition. However, only 18.5% of included trials met criteria for low risk of bias, with common limitations including small sample sizes, inability to blind participants and staff, and short follow-up periods. Larger, better-designed trials with longer follow-up are needed to establish effectiveness and guide clinical recommendations.
articles.why: These findings may inform clinical discussions about evidence-based options for patients with persistent post-COVID-19 symptoms. The consistent benefit of structured physical rehabilitation and psychological therapy could support conversations about rehabilitation pathways, while the lack of benefit for some alternative approaches may help clinicians discuss realistic expectations. The quality limitations underscore the need for caution in generalizing results to broader populations.
articles.evidence: Systematic review of randomized controlled trials. Total sample: 1,998 participants across 27 trials. Major limitations: only 18.5% of trials had low risk of bias; small sample sizes in most studies; inability to blind intervention delivery; short follow-up duration; and substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity precluding meta-analysis (narrative synthesis performed instead). Specific effect sizes and confidence intervals are not provided in the abstract.

articles.title: Uniportal versus Multiportal Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery for Minimally Invasive Esophagectomy in Esophageal Cancer: A GRADE-Assessed Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.dek: Uniportal video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (uVATS) for esophageal cancer shows potential advantages over multiportal VATS in reducing postoperative pain and pneumonia, with comparable safety outcomes.
summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated nine studies directly comparing uVATS with conventional multiportal VATS (mVATS) in adults undergoing minimally invasive esophagectomy for esophageal cancer. Searches covered major medical databases through April 2026. Binary outcomes were pooled as odds ratios and continuous outcomes as mean differences using random-effects modeling, with heterogeneity assessed via I² statistics and evidence certainty evaluated using the GRADE framework.

uVATS was associated with lower postoperative pain on day one (mean difference −2.10 on an unspecified scale), reduced postoperative pneumonia (odds ratio 0.41), and shorter hospital stay (mean difference −2.13 days) compared to mVATS. The two approaches showed no statistically significant differences in anastomotic leakage, overall complications, recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, perioperative mortality, intraoperative blood loss, or total operative time.

The authors concluded that uVATS appears feasible and safe relative to mVATS, potentially offering advantages in postoperative analgesia, pulmonary morbidity, and recovery length while maintaining comparable perioperative safety. They emphasized that evidence remains limited by high heterogeneity and predominance of observational studies, highlighting the need for multicenter randomized trials with standardized protocols and long-term oncologic follow-up.
articles.why: This comparative evidence may inform discussion among surgical teams considering approaches for minimally invasive esophagectomy. The reported reductions in postoperative pain and pneumonia could be relevant to patients' recovery profiles, though the predominantly observational evidence base limits confidence in these findings. Long-term oncologic outcomes—not addressed in this abstract—remain an important consideration for treatment selection.
articles.evidence: Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of nine comparative studies (design type of included studies not specified in abstract, though authors note predominance of observational work). Sample size: Not reported for meta-analysis. Major limitations: High heterogeneity noted (I² up to 99.3% for pain outcome), predominantly observational rather than randomized studies included, and lack of standardized measurement scales (pain scale not specified). Certainty of evidence evaluated using GRADE framework, though specific certainty ratings not provided in abstract. Long-term oncologic outcomes not addressed.

articles.tag: MATHEMATICAL EPIDEMIOLOGY; HEALTH EQUITY; RESPIRATORY INFECTIOUS DISEASE
articles.title: Ethnic inequities in mathematical models for respiratory infectious disease: A systematic review.
articles.dek: A systematic review found that only 28 infectious respiratory disease models reported results by ethnic group, revealing that mathematical epidemiological models rarely incorporate ethnic inequities despite their public health importance.
summary: This systematic review identified and categorized mathematical models of respiratory infectious disease transmission that stratified results by ethnic group. The researchers surveyed different modeling approaches used to represent ethnicity-related outcomes in disease transmission. The included studies employed three main frameworks: compartmental models (11 studies), individual-based models (12 studies), and metapopulation models (5 studies). Ethnic heterogeneities were represented either directly through ethnic group demographics, ethnicity-specific interaction patterns, and disease parameters, or indirectly through spatial differences in contact patterns or transmission.

The review found that consideration of ethnicity in mathematical infectious disease models is relatively new, with only three studies published before 2020. The authors note that the 28 included studies represent a small fraction of the overall volume of infectious disease modeling literature, suggesting that ethnicity-stratified reporting is uncommon despite documented ethnic inequities highlighted by the COVID-19 pandemic.

The authors conclude that incorporating ethnicity into mathematical models of disease transmission has potential to generate improved evidence for equitable public health responses and to reduce epidemic burden and inequities across ethnic groups. However, they indicate this field remains in early stages of development.
articles.why: This review documents a significant gap in how mathematical epidemiological models inform public health policy. Because mathematical models shape intervention planning and resource allocation decisions, their limited representation of ethnic inequities may inadvertently perpetuate disparities. Understanding how and whether models incorporate ethnicity is relevant to epidemiologists, public health planners, and policymakers considering how modeling evidence should inform equitable pandemic preparedness and response strategies.
articles.evidence: Systematic review design identifying 28 studies meeting inclusion criteria (exact search strategy, date range, and databases searched not specified in abstract). No randomization or control groups applicable to this review of modeling studies. The small number of included studies relative to total infectious disease modeling literature is noted as a major finding. Specific limitations of individual models and methods for assessing model quality are not detailed in the abstract. The review does not report effect sizes from individual studies.

articles.tag: ANTIPSYCHOTIC ADVERSE EFFECTS; EXERCISE INTERVENTION; PSYCHOTIC DISORDERS
articles.title: Exercise to enhance antipsychotic effectiveness and mitigate metabolic harm: systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.dek: Supervised exercise alongside antipsychotic medication improved negative symptoms and reduced body fat in adults with psychotic disorders, though changes were modest and evidence quality varied by outcome.
summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined 28 randomized controlled trials (n=1119) published since 2000 that tested supervised exercise interventions in people receiving antipsychotics for schizophrenia or related psychotic disorders. The review followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines and assessed study quality using the Revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool (RoB 2), pooling effects with random-effects models.

Exercise significantly improved negative symptoms (mean difference −3.078), general psychopathology (−2.178), and total PANSS score (−7.069). Positive symptoms showed no significant improvement. For metabolic outcomes, exercise reduced body weight (−1.620 kg), body fat percentage (−1.250%), and waist circumference (−1.420 cm). No significant effects emerged for systolic or diastolic blood pressure, fasting glucose, or lipid levels, with one small increase in total cholesterol.

The authors concluded that supervised exercise may be a beneficial adjunct to antipsychotic treatment, particularly for negative symptoms and body composition, though observed changes did not reach clinically meaningful thresholds. GRADE assessment rated evidence quality as moderate for negative symptoms, general psychopathology, body weight, and body fat percentage, but low to very low for other outcomes.
articles.why: Antipsychotics carry well-established cardiometabolic risks including weight gain and metabolic dysregulation. This synthesis suggests exercise could address both a core symptom domain (negative symptoms) and medication-related metabolic harm, potentially supporting discussion of behavioral interventions as part of comprehensive antipsychotic management. However, modest effect sizes and heterogeneous evidence quality warrant cautious interpretation and need for larger, rigorous trials before clinical recommendations.
articles.evidence: Randomized controlled trials (28 studies included). Sample size n=1119 across included studies. Major limitations: moderate to very low certainty of evidence across outcomes; no significant effects on blood pressure, glucose, or lipid profile; changes in body composition and psychopathology did not reach clinically meaningful thresholds; authors note need for high-quality, adequately powered RCTs using multicomponent exercise and comprehensive metabolic assessment. Variation in exercise protocols and outcome measurement across included trials not detailed in abstract.

articles.tag: MEDICAL EDUCATION; COMPETENCY ASSESSMENT; SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
articles.title: Entrustable professional activities in medical education: strategies and results - a systematic review.
articles.dek: A systematic review of 478 studies found diverse strategies for developing and implementing Entrustable Professional Activities (EPAs) in medical education, but identified modest study quality and gaps in cost-effectiveness research.
summary: This systematic review searched six electronic databases through March 2025 to characterize published evidence on strategies for developing, implementing, and assessing EPAs—a framework designed to address challenges in competence-based medical education. The review included 478 studies, predominantly from postgraduate training programs (59.6%) and conducted in the USA (51.5%).

The analysis found substantial methodological diversity in EPA implementation across studies and stakeholder groups. Approximately half the included studies (50.8%) addressed factors influencing EPA implementation, and 46.4% discussed EPA potential for improving learning and assessment practices. However, few studies examined cost-effectiveness. Quality assessment using the QATSDD tool revealed modest overall study quality.

The authors conclude that while EPA adoption is increasing across diverse medical education contexts, significant challenges remain—particularly regarding the methodological rigor of the published evidence base. The review highlights a research gap regarding cost-effectiveness and calls for higher-quality future investigations.
articles.why: EPAs represent an evolving approach to competence assessment in medical training. This overview of the literature may help educators, program directors, and researchers understand current implementation strategies, identify evidence-based approaches, and recognize where evidence quality needs strengthening before widespread adoption decisions.
articles.evidence: Systematic review of 478 observational and mixed-method studies identified through structured database searches. The abstract does not report a meta-analysis or aggregate effect sizes. Major limitations include modest quality of included studies (per QATSDD assessment), predominance of postgraduate and USA-based research (potentially limiting generalizability), and acknowledged research gaps regarding cost-effectiveness and long-term outcomes. The diversity of methodologies and contexts is noted but not quantitatively synthesized.

articles.title: A Systematic Review of Complications Following Elective Foot and Ankle Surgery.
articles.dek: A systematic review of recent studies found that complications after elective foot and ankle surgery occur frequently across multiple procedure types, with infection, wound problems, and nonunion being most common.
summary: This systematic review searched three databases (PubMed, Scopus, CINAHL) for studies published between January 2020 and June 2025 reporting postoperative complications in adults undergoing elective foot and ankle surgery. Nine studies involving 20,455 participants were included and analyzed narratively due to heterogeneity in study designs and procedures.

Complication rates varied substantially across studies: infection (0.3%–12.5%), wound healing problems (0.5%–10.0%), nonunion (0.8%–18.7%), hardware removal (3.8%–15.5%), nerve injury (0.2%–10.0%), pain or stiffness (0.8%–18.7%), and systemic complications (3.6%–7.4%). Risk factors consistently identified across multiple procedures included diabetes, obesity, smoking, and peripheral vascular disease. Higher complication rates were associated with revision surgery, prolonged operative time, and multisegment reconstruction.

The authors conclude that postoperative complications are common and arise from multiple factors with consistent patterns across different foot and ankle procedures. They suggest these findings support better risk stratification before surgery, targeted preoperative optimization strategies, and structured postoperative care protocols.
articles.why: This review synthesizes complication data across multiple foot and ankle procedures rather than examining single procedures in isolation, providing a broader perspective on postoperative risks. Identifying modifiable risk factors (smoking, obesity) and procedure-related factors (operative time, revision status) may help clinicians and patients engage in informed discussions about surgery timing, preoperative preparation, and expected recovery trajectories. The wide ranges in complication rates highlight the importance of considering patient-specific and procedure-specific contexts.
articles.evidence: Systematic review of observational and/or comparative studies published 2020–2025. Sample size: 20,455 total participants across nine included studies. Major limitations include substantial heterogeneity in study designs, procedures, outcome definitions, and follow-up periods, which necessitated narrative rather than quantitative synthesis. The abstract does not report whether individual studies were randomized or observational, nor does it indicate the quality assessment methodology or risk of bias evaluation. Publication year restriction (2020–2025) may exclude relevant earlier literature. Specific denominators for individual complication rates are not provided.
articles.journal: Journal of foot and ankle research

articles.title: Chios Mastic in Well-Controlled Hypertension: Findings From the HYPER-MASTIC Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.dek: A randomized trial found that Chios mastic supplementation did not reduce blood pressure in adults whose hypertension was already well controlled, though transcriptomic changes suggested potential vascular effects in higher-risk subgroups.
summary: The HYPER-MASTIC trial enrolled 106 adults with stable, well-controlled hypertension and variable cardiovascular risk. Participants were randomly assigned to receive low-dose Chios mastic (1500 mg/day), high-dose Chios mastic (2800 mg/day), or placebo for 3 months. The study was double-blind and placebo-controlled. Primary outcomes were changes in 24-hour ambulatory systolic and diastolic blood pressure; secondary outcomes included vascular function, oxidative stress markers, proteasome activity, and transcriptomic profiling in a high-risk subgroup.

Chios mastic was well tolerated with high adherence, confirmed by dose-dependent increases in plasma biomarkers. No significant between-group differences were observed in 24-hour systolic or diastolic blood pressure. Oxidative stress markers and proteasome activity did not change significantly across groups. However, in high-risk participants, mastic supplementation induced distinct transcriptomic changes in pathways related to endothelial junction organization and vascular integrity.

The authors concluded that Chios mastic supplementation did not lower blood pressure over 3 months in adults with well-controlled hypertension and low baseline cardiovascular risk, likely due to a ceiling effect. The transcriptomic findings suggest potentially biologically meaningful vascular effects in individuals with higher residual cardiovascular risk, warranting investigation in higher-risk populations.
articles.why: This trial addresses whether supplementation with a phytochemical having established antioxidant and vascular properties could address residual cardiovascular risk in patients whose blood pressure is already at goal. The null finding on blood pressure does not exclude benefit; the transcriptomic signal in higher-risk individuals raises the possibility that Chios mastic effects may be most relevant in populations with greater inflammatory or endothelial burden. Clinicians may find it useful to understand that adequate blood pressure control alone may not resolve underlying vascular dysfunction, and that future trials in higher-risk populations may better characterize whether mastic has a targeted role.
articles.evidence: Design: Double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial. Sample size: 106 adults. Major limitations include the 3-month duration, which may be insufficient to detect delayed vascular or molecular changes; selection of a population with well-controlled hypertension and relatively low baseline cardiovascular risk, which may obscure effects in higher-risk groups; lack of reported p-values and confidence intervals in the abstract; and unclear definition of the 'predefined high-risk subgroup' for transcriptomic analysis. The abstract does not provide trial registration information, statistical significance thresholds, or adjustment for multiple comparisons. The full-text paper was not reviewed.

articles.title: Characterizing vaginal misoprostol induction in individuals with and without severe obesity.
articles.dek: Severe obesity (BMI ≥40 kg/m²) is associated with prolonged labor induction, increased medication requirements, and lower vaginal delivery rates compared to lower BMI in individuals induced with vaginal misoprostol at term.
summary: This secondary analysis examined 1,322 individuals who received vaginal misoprostol for labor induction at term (≥37 weeks gestation with cervical dilation ≤2 cm), stratified by BMI: 1,058 (80%) with BMI <40 kg/m² and 264 (20%) with BMI ≥40 kg/m². Misoprostol was administered in 25 µg doses every three hours for up to five doses, followed by standardized oxytocin. Individuals with severe obesity more frequently started induction with a closed cervix.

After adjustment for clustering, initial cervical dilation, hypertension, and diabetes, inductions in the severe obesity group showed longer total duration (mean difference 3.5 hours), longer first stage of labor (mean difference 2.2 hours), and longer oxytocin duration (mean difference 2.5 hours). Those with BMI ≥40 kg/m² had lower odds of vaginal delivery (aOR 0.6) and required more misoprostol doses.

The authors conclude that severe obesity is associated with longer time to delivery and increased medication requirements, suggesting that alternative induction protocols warrant consideration in this population, though they note this must be balanced against increased comorbidities and obstetric morbidity.
articles.why: This characterization of induction outcomes by BMI category may inform counseling about expected labor progression and delivery mode likelihood in individuals with severe obesity. Understanding that prolonged induction and lower vaginal delivery rates occur in this group—independent of initial cervical conditions and comorbidities—could guide peripartum planning and resource allocation, and may prompt discussion of individualized induction protocols or anesthetic/operative readiness.
articles.evidence: Secondary analysis of the vaginal misoprostol arm from a cluster randomized controlled trial. Sample size: 1,322 individuals (264 with BMI ≥40 kg/m²). Design accounts for clustering and adjusted for multiple covariates using generalized estimating equations. Major limitations: secondary analysis design; inability to determine causality; no information on trial registration, full inclusion/exclusion criteria, or whether findings apply to all populations; missing detail on specific alternative induction protocols considered; no discussion of statistical power for subgroup comparisons.
